utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case Number IT-01-47-T, The Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and the Registrar who is back with us after having been absent for a few days. I would also like to greet the interpreters, the security officers, and everyone else. We'll be hearing a witness today, but before we do so there are two issues we have to deal with. Firstly, on the 11th of November, Defence counsel filed a motion for an extension of the time for providing their witness list and exhibit list. Defence counsel would like the deadline to be the 3rd of December 2004. The Defence counsel in their submissions explained to us the problems that they were encountering. The Trial Chamber will deliberate on the matter in a short while, but does the Prosecution have anything to say with regard to the extension of the time limit to the 3rd of December 2004? We should point out that initially, the deadline was the 12th of November. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have checked with our case manager, and we do not seem to have received that filing. We will endeavour to ensure that we locate that as quickly as possible, unless it may have been filed ex parte. I'm not aware of having even received that filing. So perhaps we can during the next break check with the -- internally within the Office of the Prosecutor to see if perhaps the filing was misaddressed internally and perhaps we can make a comment on that later today. But as of this point in time, not having seen the filing, I'm not in a position to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But perhaps Defence counsel has a copy. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. Good day, Mr. President. I'd just like to add something: We will make a copy immediately to provide the Prosecution with one. The submission was filed interparty, so not ex parte, but I will provide a copy to my colleague during the first break. I'd also like to point out -- I'd like to draw your attention to the last part of the motion which provides the Trial Chamber with some information with regard to translations. I would just like to point out that we are still discussing the matter with the Registry. We'll have a meeting in order to provide more information with regard to the translation situation. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. The second issue concerned the documents that were shown to the witness, Mustafa Hockic, the documents we have in this binder. We haven't rendered any decision, so I'm turning to the Defence now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, having heard this witness -- after we heard this witness, we didn't have time to suggest that the Trial Chamber render a decision about admitting into evidence all the documents that we had shown the witness. So we now suggest that the Trial Chamber admit into evidence all the documents from 1 to 47 which are listed on the document list. These are documents that we showed the witness. The main reasons for admitting them are that this witness identified each of the documents as documents from the civilian protection or as orders forwarded to the civilian protection staff, or as documents that he received from commissions in the field or he recognised them as his own personal documents, documents he had drafted. We therefore believe that all the conditions have been met to admit these documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, what is your position with regard to the 47 documents referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, as my colleague, Ms. Henry-Benjamin last week indicated, the Prosecution with respect to some of those documents does not believe that they are relevant to the charges as listed in the indictment in the current proceedings. At this point, I would be unable to identify precisely which of those 47 documents we would object to on relevance grounds. But our position is that among those 47 documents, there are certainly some documents which are not relevant in the Prosecution's submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll put this question on hold, and we would be -- we would appreciate it if you could inform us in advance of the documents you will be objecting to, and we will then deliberate on the matter at a subsequent date. If there are no other issues to be raised, we will call the witness into the courtroom. Could the usher please call the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps while the witness is being called into the courtroom, for the record, in light of the fact that one of the Judges was absent last week, the Prosecution believes that the record should reflect that all three Judges are currently present. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All three Judges are present. We take note of the fact. We acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I'd first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you give me your first and last names, your date of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Fahir Camdzic. I was born on the 10th of June 1965 in the village of Obrenovci in the Zenica Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an officer in the federation army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What rank do you hold and what is your pursuant position? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a major. I am the commander of the educational centre in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a military or civilian position? If you held a military position, where were you assigned and what rank did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I didn't have a rank, but I performed the duties of the commander of the sector staff in Mehurici in Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And were you assigned to a brigade or to a unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the time, there were no brigades. I was a member of the Territorial Defence sector staff which was under the command of the Territorial Defence municipal staff in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, the 306th Mountain Brigade was formed, and I performed the duties of the commander of the 2nd Battalion in the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in 1992 and 1993 in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never testified before. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Before Defence commences its examination, I'd like to provide you with some information about the procedures that will be followed here. The hearing should be concluded at 1.45, and I hope that you will be free at the beginning of the afternoon. You will first have to answer questions put to you by Defence counsel for the accused. They are sitting to your left. After that stage, members of the Prosecution who are to your right will conduct their cross-examination. Three Judges before you may also ask you questions. As a rule, we prefer to wait for the parties to conclude with their questions before we put questions to you. Try to provide simple answers for the questions. If you don't understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Sometimes the questions can be very complicated, which means you should take time to answer them. We have no written documents concerning your testimony, so what you say is very important. I would also like to inform you of the following: You have taken a solemn declaration, which means that you should not give false testimony. False testimony is an offence which is punishable, and a prison sentence of up to seven years could be given for false testimony. And secondly, when a witness answers a question, if the witness believes that the information he provides might be incriminating, in such a case, the witness may refuse to answer the question. But the Trial Chamber in such a case can oblige the witness to answer the question. However, the witness is granted a form of immunity in such cases. This allows a witness to feel quite free to testify. If you encounter any difficulties in the course of this hearing, do inform us of the fact and we will try to resolve them. This is how we will be proceeding today, and I know that Defence counsel has some additional information to provide you with. Defence counsel, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Camdzic. As the Presiding Judge has just said, I would like to ask you, Mr. Camdzic, to make a brief pause after I put my question to you. This will enable the interpreters to translate the question. I will also make a brief pause after your answer so we have time for your answers to be interpreted. This is very important because the Chamber and all my colleagues in the courtroom must be able to follow what is being said. Have you under me, Mr. Candzic?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were an officer in the BH Federation Army. Could you tell us about your educational background, Mr. Camdzic.

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I completed primary and secondary school in Zenica Municipality. I then went to the military academy in Belgrade, and I graduated from the military academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had graduated from the military academy, could you tell us, Mr. Camdzic, where you were assigned?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, after I had graduated, I was first assigned to the island of Vis in Croatia, and then I was -- I performed duties in Sibenik. And finally, my final post in the JNA was in Titov Drvar in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a rank in the JNA? If so, which rank did you have and what were the last duties that you performed in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The last duties that I performed in the JNA were the duties of a commander of an infantry company. And at the time, I had the rank of lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, did you at any time leave the JNA? And if so, could you tell me when and why?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I left the JNA on the 1st of April 1992. The reason for doing so was that this army was no longer the army I had been educated for. This army had become the army of one of the peoples in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left the JNA at the beginning of April, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: When I left the JNA, I went to my place of birth, to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, at that time or at any subsequent time, did you join any defence forces? And if so, which defence forces did you join and where?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Since I arrived in my place of birth, I reported to the regional Territorial Defence staff in Zenica and placed myself at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Zenica? And did you leave the Zenica area? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I stayed for a month or month and a half in Zenica. And then by order from the commander of the regional Territorial Defence staff in Zenica, I was assigned a task in the municipal Territorial Defence staff in Travnik, or rather in the Mehurici Territorial Defence sector staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which duties were you given in the Territorial Defence sector staff in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived in the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence in Travnik, I was assigned the duties of the commander of the Mehurici Territorial Defence sector staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, were you -- had you ever been in Mehurici before that date, or rather in the Bila Valley?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the commander -- the command of your sector staff located?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The command of the Territorial Defence sector staff in Mehurici was located in the Mehurici primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who provided the premises for the command of the sector staff?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, when I arrived in Mehurici, the premises for the sector staff command in Mehurici were provided by the War Presidency of the local commune in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the sector staff command use the entire school building? And if not, who else used that building?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the sector staff command in Mehurici didn't use the entire primary school building in Mehurici. On the whole, we used the offices on Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond the ground floor of the school, whereas other parts of the building were still used by the school, by the director, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As commander of the sector staff, were you able to use the remaining parts of the school?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the other parts of the school are concerned, no, we couldn't use them and it wasn't necessary for us to make use of the other parts of the school. A small number of people were located there, and the premises we had were quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, could you now tell me which places were part of the sector staff? Or rather, which villages in the Bila Valley were covered by the Mehurici sector staff, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try and list all the villages covered by the sector staff. There were the villages of Jezerci, Fazlici, Zagradje, Gornja and Donja Orahovo, Bukovica, Velika Bukovica, Visnjevo, Dub, Suhi Do, Poljanice, and Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the sector staff command was located in the primary school. Could you tell us where the combatants who were members of the sector staff were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, all the combatants who weren't at the positions facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor stayed in their homes. We didn't have any barracks. We didn't have any facilities in which we could accommodate the entire unit. Once they had finished their shift, they would return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, could you tell us how you mobilised the population into the sector staff, or rather into the companies that were part of the sector staff?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, initially, men who had joined the companies were mobilised from villages. The secretariat mobilised them. The secretariat for national defence in Travnik Municipality. I was just provided with these combatants who had been called up by the secretariat for national defence in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, Mr. Camdzic, did Croats in your area also receive these call-up papers and did they join the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure, but as far as I know, they, too, were called up. However, they never responded to the call-up. They never joined the Territorial Defence units that were under my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they organised themselves in a military manner? And if so, do you know which units they joined?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, they formed their own units. While I was up there, there were HOS units and HVO units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were an officer in the JNA when you assumed the duties you have mentioned. Could you tell us what sort of equipment your units had. I'm referring primarily to weapons and uniforms.

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA had been fully equipped, but when I assumed my new duties, these units had no weapons and hardly any uniforms. And most of the weapons were hunting rifles that the inhabitants had at the time, and they had licenses for these weapons. But there were very few weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As commander of the sector staff, you were probably aware of how the other Territorial Defence units in the area of your municipality were armed. Were they in a better situation than the situation that your combatants were in?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the Territorial Defence as a whole in the Travnik Municipality, as far as I know, was not in a better situation when compared to the unit that I was in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard evidence about the fact that before the war, the Territorial Defence had weapons of its own. Could you tell us whether you know what happened to the Territorial Defence weapons and why these weapons weren't handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA, in addition to regular units, paid a lot of attention to Territorial Defence units. That's how it was formed. That's how the JNA was formed. So in the area of Travnik, there were weapons that belonged to the Territorial Defence. And at some point in time, JNA units assumed control over these weapons. These weapons were located in the barracks in Slimena -- were located in the Slimena barracks that used to belong to the JNA. Pressure was exerted so that these weapons could be taken, and the JNA officers who were there didn't want to hand over these weapons. So the warehouse, or rather warehouses in which these weapons were located were blown up. They blew these warehouses up. They destroyed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while ago you've told us that the Croatian population in that area organised themselves into the HOS and the HVO. Compare those to your units and tell us what weapons and equipment the HOS and the HVO had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: When you compare them to us, they were much better equipped and much better armed. We envied them because all of them had modern weapons. I'm now referring to rifles, automatic rifles, machine-guns and so on and so forth. They were much better armed than we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the sector staff in Mehurici was functioning, did you take place in combat, and where was that?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: While I worked in the sector staff in Mehurici, I spent most of my time on the line facing the Chetniks. This line was active all the time. There were daily combat operations there. We were mostly engaged in defence because we were under constant Chetnik attacks. So I spent most of the time on the Vlasic plateau, on the line facing the Chetniks there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were the commander of the sector staff and subsequently, did the Territorial Defence take the overall command in the territory of local communes that fell under your sector?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Not only in my sector, but in the whole territory of the municipality of Travnik. The Territorial Defence never took control or power in those areas. We did what we were told to do by the War Presidency in Travnik Municipality, and the War Presidency was in control and had power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, in the summer of 1992, were there any changes within the Territorial Defence? And did the units become larger and bigger?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: In mid-1992 in the month of July, the sector staffs in the municipality were transformed. This was done pursuant to the order of the commander. Sector staff stopped being active, and they were transformed into detachments in the whole of the area of Travnik Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many detachments were established in the Bila Valley? Did you keep any of the positions in any of the Territorial Defence detachments?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: In the Bila Valley, four detachments were established. I remained in the position of the commander of the Mehurici detachment, detachments which were established. From Mehurici, there were two of them. One of them was Luta Greda, and another one was Mehurici, and there was another detachment called Hum and another one called Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the command of that detachment?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The command of my detachment remained in the school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the accommodation of members of your detachment? Were there any changes with regard to the previous situation?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: There were no changes. Everything remained the same. The only thing that changed was the name. It was no longer the sector staff. It was now the Mehurici detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, I would like to move on to some other topics. In your capacity as the commander of the sector staff or the commander of the detachment, did you notice some foreigners appearing in Travnik Municipality in the area covered by your detachment?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed some foreigners. I don't know where from and how. As I've already told you, I spent most of my time on the Vlasic plateau, on the line there. So when I went back, I did notice some foreigners, and the period in question was maybe the end of summer or the beginning of autumn. And this is where I saw for the first time that some foreigners had arrived in the area of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn, did you find out where these foreigners were accommodated? First, let me ask you who these foreigners were and what countries they had arrived from. Were you aware of that? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know where they had come from. But judging by the way they looked and judging by the way they were dressed, I could conclude that they were foreigners from Arabic countries. I don't know exactly where they came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you to respond to my previous question, and the question was whether you know where they were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: When they arrived in Mehurici, they were accommodated in the same school in Mehurici where my command post was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they accommodated on the ground floor, in the offices on the ground floor where your detachment was as well?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No. They were given the second and the third floor of the elementary school. So they didn't share any of the offices that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that you noticed those foreigners once you returned from your longer stay on the line. Did you react to the fact that all of a sudden there were some foreigners in the school where your command was?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Of course I reacted immediately. Since my command post was there, I said that we did not feel safe with those foreigners so close to us. I informed my immediate superior commander about the situation, and I asked him what to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior at the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: At that time, my immediate superior commander was the commander of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Travnik, Mr. Haso Ribo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of the fact that you've already told us that you were not in charge of allocating space, as the commander of the sector staff, did you approach some civilian bodies in Mehurici or elsewhere with regard to this problem?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did try to talk to the president of the War Presidency of Mehurici. I wanted to see why these people were billeted there. He was the representative of the civilian power which was in full control, and it seems that he had ordered the principal of the school to give these people accommodation. I tried to talk to this man in order to find a solution. It was not in my best interests to have these people so close to me. However, I didn't manage to persuade the president of the War Presidency to move those people from the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did these foreigners introduce themselves to you? Did they tell you what their reason for being there was? Did anybody from the civilian bodies of power tell you what was their relationship with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: In my conversation with the president of the War Presidency, he told me that those people were representatives of humanitarian organisations, that we needed them there because they would help us with our problem of food and so on and so forth. So they were supposed to help the civilian population. They were supposed to provide them with food items and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did people in your vicinity call these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: They started by calling them Arabs, just like I did. That's how we recognised them, as Arabs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, at any point in time, did the customary name used by the population change?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime later, these Arabs and foreigners started being called the mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the commander of the Mehurici detachment. And just for the record, this was in autumn 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since people called them Arabs and since you learned from the civilian bodies that they were humanitarian workers, were you aware of the fact that in autumn 1992, they indeed played a humanitarian role, that they provided people with packages, with food, and everyone else that would fall within the scope of humanitarian activities?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, they really did that. They collected and distributed various packages containing all sorts of things, mainly food items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give anything to your sector staff, i.e., to the Territorial Defence? Did they provide any logistical support to you?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No, no. They never provided me with any logistical support. They even avoided any contact with me. I don't know why. They probably didn't trust me or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that at one point in time, they were given the name mujahedin. You graduated from the military academy, and you were a JNA officer. What did you know about the mujahedin, who the mujahedin were?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: In the country and in the regions where I had resided up to then, I never heard this word mujahedin, and I didn't what this word represented. It was a foreign word to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, do you know whether these foreigners, the mujahedin, ever changed their place of stay? If you're aware of that, can you tell us when and why this happened?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: When the Territorial Defence units were reorganised, the corps were established within the BiH Army. In the Bila Valley, the 306th Mountain Brigade was established. At the very beginning of the establishment of the 306th Mountain Brigade, the foreigners who had been accommodated in Mehurici, in the school in Mehurici, they started leaving the school, and they moved to Poljanice village, some 900 metres from the elementary school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just mentioned some changes in the organisation of the army and the establishment of the 306th Mountain Brigade. Which units became part of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The 306th Mountain Brigade was composed of all the former detachments plus a unit which had been formed from the ranks of the refugees who had come from Kotor Varos, and this unit was called and was best known as the Siprage Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your knowledge and information, Mr. Camdzic, at the beginning when the 306th Brigade was first established, were there any problems? Did some of the population join some other units or brigades of the BiH Army?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The mere fact that the 306th Brigade was established didn't mean that there were no problems. These problems that existed primarily had to do with the villages of Gluha Bukovica and Zagradje, which refused to put themselves on the strength of the 306th Mountain Brigade. These villages wanted to be on the strength of some other unit. And after several rounds of negotiations, requests, and demands, these two villages were put on the strength of the 314th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, at that point in time, did you take over another duty or position? And if that is the case, what was that position?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: When the 306th Mountain Brigade was established, I assumed a new position. I became the commander of the 2nd Battalion on the strength of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the command post of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The command post of my battalion was in Krpeljici village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that some other unit of the 306th Mountain Brigade remained in the primary school in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: When the 306th Mountain Brigade was established, a unit of the Siprage Battalion entered the Mehurici primary school and made it its command post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, from which areas of the Bila Valley were people recruited for the 2nd Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade was replenished from the areas from which the Hum detachment was replenished. The following villages, Krpeljici, Maline, Velika Bukovica, Mosur, Bandol, and Radojicici were the villages from which our recruits came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the soldiers of your battalion billeted? Did you have anything that would be known as the barracks of the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No. As a unit, we never had our own barracks. Our members stayed at home. They stayed in their houses. Just as was the case in the sector staff and in the detachment that I belonged prior to that. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the 2nd Battalion was established, did you manage to replenish it to the full strength? Did you have weapons? Did you have the necessary military equipment? Did you have all the necessary staff?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: It would have been only too good if I had been able to do that. However, I could never bring the battalion to the full strength in terms of men, weapons, ammunition, uniforms. I never had everything that was foreseen for a unit of that strength.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men did you have? How many pieces of weaponry did you have?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: At the time, I had about 440 men. And I had about 120 rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the people at your disposal? Did you have officers? Did you have the necessary staff to perform all of the duties in the battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No, we did not have educated officers. It was mostly replenished from the ranks of the people who had served in the former JNA who had some experience. They did not have any higher ranks. The highest rank was a lance corporal, the lance corporal of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What rank should be the officer in command of a battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: In normal conditions, the commander of a battalion should be a major. That is the lowest possible rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not have a rank. I didn't have any rank of the BiH Army. I had the rank of lieutenant from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to yourself, how many officers were in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that there were no higher ranking officers in my battalion. There were neither officers or noncommissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any logistical reserves? Did you have reserve ammunition for your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No, we did not have any reserves. Whatever we had in terms of ammunition and weapons was on the defence line facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under such conditions, how did you establish the chain of command between you as the commander and your soldiers? In other words, between the superior commands and the subordinate commands?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The system of command and control in those conditions was very difficult to establish. We could communicate to a certain extent with our superiors. However, when it came to our subordinates, the communication was not so easy. We did not have enough communication means or other means that might have facilitated this communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the human resources that you had at your disposal, and you've just told us that these people were not prepared for war, can you tell us whether in the battalion, in the brigade, or elsewhere, was any sort of training carried out? If that was the case, can you tell me who organised this training and how it was done?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: At the level of the brigade command, an order was issued and plans were drafted for our training and education. However, this training could not be organised easily because of the constant obligations that we had on the line and the obligations of the soldiers on leave who would go back to their homes but had to do stuff at home, they had to provide their families with food and all the other bare necessities. So they had to make up for the time they spent on the line or the time they would spend on the line. The training that we could carry out in our battalion, I was in charge of that because I was the only one with some sort of a military education.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The foreigners you have referred to, did they ever train members of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No. They never trained anyone in my battalion, and they weren't present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you left Mehurici and you went to Krpeljici with your battalion command, tell me whether you yourself had any problems in the battalion as a result of the presence of the foreigners, or rather, given that you were one of the commanders of the 306th Brigade, did you ever find out or notice that the presence of these foreigners caused certain problems in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. You left Mehurici and went to Krpeljici. As the commander of the 2nd Battalion, did you ever come across problems caused by these mujahedin in the area covered by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I had some problems with regard to my battalion members and these mujahedin. The mujahedin were initially involved in humanitarian work, and they would distribute aid packets. I wasn't in a position to do this. So it was a problem to replenish the unit if someone left. But luckily, I didn't have many such cases in the battalion. But when I was part of the detachment, during that time, we had a lot of problems. Quite a few of them wanted to leave; they did leave. As to what they gave them, well, there were probably some men to whom they would also give money in order to ensure that they stood by them, that they followed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you about something else so that we can gain better insight into the situation. At the beginning of your testimony, you said that on the whole, the Croatian population joined the HVO, or rather, the HOS, the Croatian Armed Forces. Tell me, where were HVO units deployed? And where did they establish defence lines facing the common enemy?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: As far as the HVO and the HOS are concerned, while I was present in Mehurici, I'm not quite sure where they established lines, facing the Chetniks or rather, the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. But when I arrived or when I joined the 2nd Battalion, their defence lines were behind us. Perhaps 1 to 2 kilometres behind our defence lines that had been established on the Vlasic plateau.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Establishing lines behind the BH Army positions, did this cause certain concern among the combatants and the officers in the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. Naturally this made us a little concerned, a little restless. Because if we were fighting an enemy together, it would have been logical for us to have been deployed on a certain lines and not to have lines behind us. There might be reserve units behind us, but while we were at the first lines facing the Chetniks, they were behind us. And we didn't really understand the reason for this. It wasn't very clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that fact, in 1993, did the HVO conduct itself in a way that prevented you from performing your duties as battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, in the autumn of 1992, when there were certain incidents around Novi Travnik and at the beginning of 1993, too, when there were certain misunderstandings, and later with the passage of time, I had more and more problems with the HVO. Since in 1993, from March -- or perhaps even before, I couldn't rotate my men in a normal way. Nothing could be done without announcing one's intentions for they had established checkpoints around Vlasic. And it was necessary to announce our intention to pass through. So this made the situation difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of contact was there with the basic centres in Travnik and Zenica, and were there any problems as far as your battalion was concerned in that sense, too?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the communications, as far as my battalion is concerned, I can say that I had problems when I had to communicate with the superior command. And naturally, when it was necessary to go to Zenica or to Travnik, this was so difficult -- it was so difficult that one felt that an incident would occur at any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any orders with regard to those incidents? And if so, what kind of orders? What was the army's position with regard to the possibility of a conflict with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I had received specific orders from my commander according to which we were to avoid incidents of any kind, whatever the cost. We were supposed to avoid anything that might provoke a conflict in the area with our allies. At the time, they were our allies. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO realise the efforts made by the 306th Brigade above all, but he could also say by the BH Army, and did the HVO try to avoid conflicts? And if not, how did the HVO behave?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say whether the HVO was making efforts of any kind or not. The situation in the field seemed to point to the contrary. There were no changes. Perhaps some sort of a joint command had been formed at our level, but if an order of some kind was issued, well, I personally didn't notice that they had the desire to act in the way that we were acting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, at any point in time did the way the HVO was behaving make it impossible for you to reach your own command post? And if that was the case, could you tell us a little more about it.

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. On one occasion, I left my command post to visit the unit in Maline. I was maltreated when I left. I was maltreated by the HVO. I must emphasise the fact, since I passed through Guca Gora, that's when I first saw some new individuals. They weren't the inhabitants of Guca Gora, but they were people who had been brought there from somewhere in order to create a certain kind of situation. On the whole, these were young men up to about 17 years of age. I'll just provide you with one example. Once they pulled me out of the car, they searched me. So in spite of the fact that I had a pistol on me, they didn't find it. It hadn't been concealed, but they didn't find the pistol. So perhaps these young men had been brought there to provoke such incidents. Then they drove me out of the -- drove me away towards the village of Maline. They said I shouldn't return and said that it would be possible only for me to return to my place. I don't think they knew that I was the commander of the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The young men who stopped you, which units were they a member of? Were they members of the army or some other formation?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, if they had been army members, they certainly wouldn't have stopped me. They were HVO members. They had HVO insignia on them. As to the unit they belonged to within the HVO, I really don't know. In Guca Gora, in the Guca Gora area, there was the Frankopan Brigade. I don't think they were members of this brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, tell me now, how did the situation develop in May 1993? And what happened to your battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, in the village of Ahmici in May 1993, what happened there affected the entire region. In May, there were large-scale blockades, and my battalion, from May until the end, was practically no longer functioning as a battalion. These units were village units which were surrounded by the HVO and by the Croatian side, and they had been abandoned to themselves. As far as communications and command is concerned, it wasn't functioning. These command and communications were not efficient. I had some sort of a Motorola, but there was no one in the command to whom I could assign the duty of controlling that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you still holding the lines on the Vlasic plateau, and what sort of problems were there as a result of the blockade of your battalion in certain villages?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: In spite of everything that was happening down there, I had a zone of responsibility facing the Chetniks. That's where my unit was. My unit had remained in that area. And there was a serious problem that arose since, from May until mid-June, I couldn't rotate the men who were there. Given the situation in the field, given the fact that we had dugouts at the positions, and the soldiers couldn't wash themselves, there wasn't enough food, given the fact that I couldn't reach them because this was very difficult, the company commander kept trying to convince me to rotate the men. But the situation was particularly difficult when the first clashes with the HVO occurred. The situation was difficult because the families of these soldiers who had remained up there, well, these soldiers had been left to their own devices. So the situation was very difficult for the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first started performing the duties of the commander of the 2nd Battalion, you told me which villages had men who were recruited into the battalion. Now you say that most of the villages were surrounded. Tell me which villages you were not able to communicate with, and in which villages did you have some men from your battalion -- some of the men from your battalion who were on leave?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any physical contact with the unit, or rather, the village of Maline. It wasn't possible for me to go to the village of Radojcici. I couldn't go to the village of Bandol. I couldn't go to the village of Velika Bukovica. I could only go to the village of Mosur and Krpeljici, and at great risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did your men have? I'm referring to the men who were in the villages that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, on the whole, they had hunting rifles, and some weapons that inhabitants had managed to buy on the street, on the black market. Many people would sell the last cow they had to obtain weapons, so they didn't have sufficient weapons to mount an effective defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, at the beginning of June, where was the commander of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of June, the commander of my brigade was in the village of Krpeljici, which is where I was, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't he go to the command post in Rudnik?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't go to the command post in Rudnik because all the roads used to reach Rudnik had been blocked. And I really didn't know how he ended up in Krpeljici because to get to Krpeljici from Travnik, it would have been necessary for him to pass through at least two HVO checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men from the 2nd Battalion were in the village of Krpeljici at the beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning of June, the soldiers in the village of Krpeljici were from that area, and those who had not been engaged to fight the Chetniks were there. I think there were about 80 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a battalion commander, did you receive any information from your soldiers who were in these surrounded villages?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was constantly receiving bad news from Velika Bukovica. From the 30th of May onwards, they kept requesting assistance. They were afraid. They were surrounded. They thought that something was going to happen on the 4th of June. The situation was dramatic. Attacks were launched against them. For the first hour or so, they asked for assistance while they were able to use a radio link to do so. But after an hour had passed, I no longer received any news from up there. I thought it was all over. From the position I was at, at Krpeljici, from that position I could hear loud explosions. I could hear fierce shooting. Assistance was requested, but there was nothing we could do to help these men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why wasn't it possible for the 80 combatants from Krpeljici to go to help the combatants and the people in Velika Bukovica?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the 80 soldiers who were there couldn't do anything for two reasons: First of all, and this is the main reason: In my opinion, the depth was great. And with such a small number of men, we couldn't pass through the HVO defence line which was above Krpeljici. With such a small number of men, it was impossible to pass through such an area and reach those men. And the second reason is that we couldn't allow the defence line we were at to be weakened. Since we were surrounded, we couldn't spare men for Velika Bukovica without endangering the security of the people. So they were defending their village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a battalion commander, did you request assistance? And if so, who did you make such a request to?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked my brigade commander to provide us with assistance, since he was there. I asked him to see how we could deal with the situation. But since the commander wasn't able to establish communications, everything went through my command post. He immediately forwarded a request to the 1st Battalion in Mehurici. And I think the 4th Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Battalion was also there. He requested that the commanders of those units attempt to assist the men in Velika Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the fact that you're aware of the tragedy taking place in Velika Bukovica, did you find out about the HVO attacking any other areas in which your men who were on leave had been blocked?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Well, in addition to what happened on Bukovica, the HVO continued exerting pressure on all the other places. And in particular, on the 7th of June, the village of Maline was attacked by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in time did the available units of the 306th Brigade accept to implement the request of the command, and do you know what happened in that area on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: As soon as we forwarded this request for assistance on the 4th of June, well, nothing happened. We weren't told that anyone would go to assist these men. And this was the situation right up until the 6th, and even later. There was nothing to indicate that someone was going to assist us. We were doing everything we could to organise ourselves as best as possible. And later, on the basis of HVO documents that I obtained, I saw that there was a plan for an attack. And according to the plan, they were to take one village after the other. I'm referring to Bosniak villages. And in this manner, they were to establish full control of the area that we were in. So when I now examine how this started, Velika Bukovica on the 4th, Maline on the 7th. That's when these places were attacked. Well, we were getting prepared, but I didn't expect any assistance on the 8th. Men from Mehurici came on that date and lifted the blockade of our units that were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Camdzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps this is a good time for a break. But would the Trial Chamber allow me to examine this witness for a little more than an hour and a half. I will shorten the examination of the witness for tomorrow, and I believe that I will be able to conclude my examination of both witnesses in the time -- within the time limit planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's half past 10.00. We will resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, before the break, we were talking about the events on the 8th of June. When and where did you receive information about certain successes of the units that went to help the fighters of your battalion who were encircled?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I didn't have any information whatsoever. The first news of these successes came to me directly when we were deblocked from the north, from the direction of Guca Gora. Our forces which had been encircled linked up with the forces that were moving from the direction of Mehurici. It was only then that I knew that we had success, that we were finally deblocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Camdzic, did you start to establish gradual links with your fighters who had been blocked in the general area? At that point in time, did you issue orders to your fighters? Did you give them any tasks?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first thing I wanted to do at that time was to consolidate our ranks. I wanted us to be a unit again. The first tasks that I gave to those units which were deblocked on that day were to immediately link up. I wanted us to establish a communication, a line, and to have full control of the entire unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as we know from the testimonies that we've heard so far, Krpeljici is very close to Guca Gora. Did you or your men at any point in time enter Guca Gora? Did you continue combat operations even after the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, between the 8th of June and the 10th of June, we were mostly busy with the consolidation of our ranks and the establishment of communication and command in our units. On the 10th of June, we continued activities. And on the 10th of June, we entered Guca Gora. We passed through Guca Gora, in other words, and we stayed on the lines that were subsequently formed. That's where we stayed until the end of that conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how many days subsequent to that did your men participate in combat operations facing the positions of the HVO, Nova Bila, and other areas that you wanted to liberate?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Once the line was established in this area, once we carried out the complete deblocking and once we managed to link up all the villages from which the second battalion was recruited and replenished, we continued moving towards the place called Kostrum [as interpreted]. Between the 10th and the 14th of June, we had some activities there because that place was directly on the road leading from Travnik up to Zenica. This road was still under blockade and was still not passable. One could still not use it to go towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the 8th and the 10th when you tried to establish communication with your fighters and your companies, from that day on, did you know where parts of your battalion were? Were you aware of the whereabouts of all the companies of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. From that day on, I had all of my units on the strength, although I can't say that the control was full, to the extent it would be later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to your previous answer. You said that you entered Guca Gora. In Guca Gora itself at the moment when you entered it, were there any combat operations taking place? Did you find the population of Guca Gora there?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No. When we entered Guca Gora, we did it without a bullet fired. There was no fighting. The population had already left Guca Gora probably on the 8th or on the 9th of June. Guca Gora was, therefore, completely empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were passing through Guca Gora, did you notice any significant damage or any damage at all? Were there any burnt-down houses or anything that could testify to the combat operations that had taken place between the 8th and the 10th of June?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Between the 8th and the 10th of June, during the combat operations that were taking place, I was, together with my men, as we were walking through Guca Gora, as we were moving through Guca Gora, and I couldn't see any damages. There may have been some burnt-down stables and cow sheds, and I suppose that this happened on the 8th of June during the combat operations. The rest of the village was intact. There were no damages. Everything looked normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered Guca Gora, did you get hold of some of the documents that belonged to the Frankopan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document that you mentioned a while ago, was it a part of that documentation?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I can't remember whether it was part of those documents, of that archive of the Frankopan Brigade. But when this area was being liberated, wherever we liberated places, the document must have been there. I did not personally see it as part of that documentation. One of the fighters actually brought this document to me, and that's when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given your previous answers, I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit P690. That's the Prosecution Exhibit P690.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you look at the document and before I put a question to you, can you please look at the last page. Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The document was signed by Commander Sipic who was the commander of the 306th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document, and then I will ask you a couple of questions. Can you please pay special attention to item 4 and the last sentence where it says "readiness for attack, 1100 hours on the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond 13th of June," and also to items 5.4 and 5.5. Have you had a look at these items?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you took over the command and that you knew exactly where the units were. Under 5.4 and 5.5, what does 2/306 refer to?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Under 5.4, this would refer to one part of my battalion, the 2nd Battalion of 306th, whereas under item 5.5, the Mosur Company is a reference to one part of my battalion. It seems here that I am the commander of the entire battalion, and still the brigade commander issues orders to parts of my battalion. That is not conceivable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I see it for the first time. I have never received this document before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told me that you knew where your units were. Would items 5.4 and 5.5 reflect that? Would it correspond to what you have just told us, and that is that you knew exactly where your units were?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The deployment of units corresponds to this item 5.4. However, this is an assault order, and we did not engage in any assault. We were holding a defence line. We were not on the attack line. I don't know what the commander's idea was. Maybe he had an idea to do something of that sort. I never received this order. And on that day, when this combat readiness at 1100 hours is mentioned, I can claim with full certainty that we were not getting ready for any attack. We were not on any of the lines from which an attack was launched on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, do you know Dervis Suljic?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what his position in the brigade was?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: At this time here, he was the assistant commander for intelligence. Actually, he was the assistant chief of staff for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he exercise command over any units?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while ago spontaneously, you said that you don't know why the commander would issue orders to your companies. Why do you find it inconceivable for a brigade commander to issue such orders? Is there any other way in which units of certain battalions are engaged?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: This is inconceivable because the commander does not have to go that low down the chain. He doesn't have to issue orders to lower ranking units if I am their commander. It would be normal for him to issue orders to me. If he had some idea to do something, he could have established a tactical group, and then some units could be resubordinated to that tactical group in order to carry out an order. However, as far as I know, on that day during that time there was no tactical group, there was nothing put the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Camdzic, are you aware of the fact that with regard to all the problems that we have mentioned, that an order was drafted, and it was never implemented, never carried out? Was that a common occurrence?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were such situations. In my battalion, I personally encountered such situations. There were written orders which were not carried out for several reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, as far as you and your units are concerned, the ones that are described herein, is this a combat order that you received and that was carried out?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: No. This is a combat order, an order for attack. However, I never saw it before, and we didn't do anything on that day pursuant to this order. My unit, my battalion, did not do anything to this effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now let's go back to Guca Gora. First of all, tell me how big is Guca Gora? Can you give me some indication? How many houses are there in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Guca Gora is a somewhat bigger settlement, and the population was Croatian. There are about 250 houses in Guca Gora. That would be the indication of its size.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you established your lines facing the HVO south of Guca Gora towards Nova Bila, did combat operations on those lines continue, and for how long? How long did combat operations last in that area?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of June, we stopped and established our lines. And those lines were never changed after that. They were neither moved forward or backward. Those lines were active on a daily basis. There were daily assaults on both sides. We carried out a few attacks, but we were pushed back and vice versa. Until the moment the Washington Agreement was signed, these lines were active. There were activities on those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Guca Gora from those lines? Is Guca Gora within the range of fire from those lines?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: The distance between Guca Gora and those lines is approximately 2.5 to 3 kilometres, and it is certainly within the fire range. So all the artillery pieces that were on the line could open fire on Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, do you have any personal information or knowledge about what happened from then on? Was there any shelling or attack on Guca Gora from the HVO lines? Were there any consequences due to such combat operations?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: In autumn, I became a member of the command of 306th Brigade. I personally saw things that I didn't approve of. On one day, I don't know when it was, the church in Guca Gora was shelled. Below the church and the monastery, some 200 or 300 metres south of the church, some facilities were shelled, some houses were shelled, and some ten houses were set on fire as a result of the HVO shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, did you as a member of the command of the 306th Brigade know anything about the looting and torching of some houses during that period when you were there in the area?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of those things. I was aware of the looting and torching of the houses in Guca Gora. The brigade commander did take measures in order to prevent such incidents. When houses were torched, it usually happened either in the evening or during the night when it was very difficult to control the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Camdzic, were there only troops moving through the area, or were there also some other people moving through the area or coming to the area under the control of the 306th Brigade and especially Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were civilians moving from all over the place. They came from all over the place as a result of the very difficult situation that the population was in. A lot of people came from the territory of Zenica. They passed through Guca Gora moving further. They were looking for flour. They moved on foot all the way up to Bugojno. There were people moving around every day. They would come from different corners of the free territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the monastery in Guca Gora, are you aware of any orders issued by your commander? How were these orders carried out?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I am speaking as a battalion commander who received direct orders from the brigade commander. We had very specific orders to protect houses from torching, that special attention should be paid to the monastery and the church in Guca Gora in order to prevent destruction and damage. We had a specific order to prevent looting and plunder. We were told what we were not supposed to do as a unit. As we were entering Guca Gora, I decided on purpose to be close to my men in order to be able to carry out the brigade commander's orders as well as possible. While I was there, I can tell you that I had things under full control. Later on, another order arrived according to which the security for the church and the monastery should be provided by the military police platoon which was on the strength of the 306th Brigade, and that was their subsequent role. The military police secured this facility in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given the situation that you have just described, did at any point in time an order arrive for the brigade command to be accommodated in the general area of the monastery in order to provide for its protection?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. At that time, I was already a member of the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond brigade command. We were not absolutely sure that the military police would carry out their task properly. And still, we wanted to protect the monastery and the church in Guca Gora, and that's why the commander decided that we should be accommodated in the offices that existed in the monastery in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is telling me that there is something that might have been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when were you the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I was the battalion commander up to the end of August or beginning of September 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, what position did you take?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: I became the operations person in the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The brigade command?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is now clear and the possible error has been rectified. Just a few more questions, Mr. Camdzic: You've told us that parts of your brigade were encircled in the villages of Velika Bukovica and Bandol and that from the 4th of June, terrible news reached you from Velika Bukovica and also that you heard that this place was being shelled. Can you tell us, please, whether your units finally managed to enter Velika Bukovica and Bandol, and when they did, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Our units entered Velika Bukovica on the 8th. Nothing was found there, in fact. Only burnt houses. I was afraid that we wouldn't find civilians there. However, on that morning, HVO members took the civilian population of Velika Bukovica away and used them as a human shield, and they withdrew in the direction of Nova Bila. As far as Bandol was concerned, we entered Bandol on the 14th when we had taken Gostinj, too. And it was terrible. There, everything had been burnt down. There was a mosque there over a hundred years old. It had also burnt down. So nothing was left intact there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Camdzic, could you tell me whether the foreigners we have spoken about, the mujahedin, did they at any time while you were the battalion commander or a member of the 306th Brigade Command, or rather were they at any time under the command of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: While I was the battalion commander, this was never the case in my battalion. And when I joined the 306th Brigade Mountain Brigade, they were never part of the units of the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Camdzic, could you tell me about the brigade's attitude towards violations of the law by army members pursuant to orders issued by the 3rd Corps. What sort of measures were taken to deal with violations, looting, torching, et cetera? What sort of measures were taken to punish the perpetrators of such acts, and what sort of orders were issued by the 3rd Corps command to this effect?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: We did everything that we were allowed to do. We took disciplinary measures, and this usually involved military detention for all those who had been identified as perpetrators. As for more serious violations, criminal reports were filed with the court in Travnik. I wasn't in such a position to know who these individuals were, but I am certain that these cases were dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Camdzic. Mr. President, I have concluded my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a few questions for this witness. Cross-examined by Mr. Ibrisimovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Camdzic, at the beginning of your testimony today you said that you graduated from the military academy in Belgrade. You were involved in land forces.

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you served as a JNA officer in Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the war, you already had a certain amount of professional experience as an officer?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Afterwards, you became a detachment commander in the Mehurici sector staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That detachment became part of the 306th Brigade after this brigade had been formed, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You became the commander of the 2nd Battalion in the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to my colleague's question, you said that the battalion command was located in the village of Krpeljici?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the battalion commander, you were certainly informed of the fact that in your battalion's zone of responsibility there were some other BH Army unit that was active. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHIR CAMDZIC
